analysis.answer: Current law allows parents to receive 90 percent of state per-pupil funding in an education savings account to pay for private education expenses. The proposed measure repeals this program entirely on July 1, 2028, and transfers any unspent funds back to the state school fund.

Public school districts benefit by retaining full per-pupil funding for students who might have otherwise left, and by receiving any unspent funds from the accounts. Families who use or planned to use the accounts for private tuition or tutoring bear the cost of losing state financial support for those alternatives.

Families relying on the accounts may shift their children back into the public school system or bear the full cost of private alternatives. Private schools, tutors, and online course providers may experience reduced demand and enrollment.

The measure addresses concerns that the education savings account program redirects state funds away from the public school system. By repealing the program, the mechanism halts this diversion, but in doing so, it removes a financial mechanism designed to help families afford alternative educational options.

The financial and educational impacts of education savings accounts are disputed. Some researchers find that such programs reduce resources available to public schools and can lead to negative or mixed academic outcomes for participating students. Other researchers find that because the accounts are funded at a fraction of total per-pupil costs (90 percent under current law), they generate net savings for the state, and that the resulting competition improves public school performance.
The measure is a statutory change that sets a future effective date of July 1, 2028, meaning the legislature could amend or reverse the repeal before the program actually ends.

flags.note: The measure includes a delayed effective date, allowing the program to continue operating for several years before the repeal takes effect.
